transcript:
# Day 17, Strategy: Sun Tzu, the supreme excellence is winning without fighting (The Art of War, chapter 3, roughly 5th century BC)

You are a product manager at a bank. A competitor just launched a feature that looks a lot like your Easy Pay offer, and the room wants a response by Friday. Match their price. Launch a counter campaign. Fight. Now picture a second room, one where nobody has to fight because the competitor looked at your partner contracts, your approval rates and your customer base and decided the fight was not worth starting. Which room would you rather be in?

Sun Tzu's chapter 3, usually translated as "Attack by Stratagem" or "Planning Offensives," is about getting into the second room. The famous line is that winning a hundred battles is not the height of skill. The height of skill is to subdue the enemy without fighting at all. He then ranks the ways to beat an opponent. Best is to defeat their plans before they are even in motion. Next is to break up their alliances. Below that is to beat their army in the field. The worst option, saved for when nothing else will do, is to besiege a walled city, because it is slow, bloody and expensive even when it works.

The core idea is simple once you see it. Fighting is a cost, not a goal. Every actual battle burns resources, invites luck into the result, and leaves the winner weaker than before. So the strategist's real job is to arrange things so the outcome is settled before the clash. Sun Tzu's word for the enemy's plans, "mou," covers their strategy, their intentions and their calculations. If you can make an opponent conclude that attacking you is pointless, you have won the war that never happened.

One business example. When Amazon announced it was entering a market, rival stock prices often fell before Amazon had sold a single item. That drop was the "attack on plans" in action. Investors, suppliers and partners revised their expectations, and some competitors quietly stopped investing. Amazon did not always follow through, which is part of the point. The reputation did the work. You saw the same thing in the Cold War, where the whole logic of deterrence was to make the fight unthinkable rather than to win it.

Now the honest objection. Winning without fighting can become an excuse for never deciding anything. Clausewitz, who we will meet later in this track, argued that war is dominated by friction, chance and the will to fight, and that clever maneuvering alone rarely ends a serious conflict. He warned that bloodless victories are often the result of one side simply being much stronger, not of superior cunning. History backs him up more than Sun Tzu fans like to admit. Hitler's bloodless wins in 1938 did not avoid a war, they delayed and enlarged it. Sun Tzu's defenders answer that he never said avoid fighting at all costs. He said fighting is the last and worst tool, and that the ranking of options is the point. Even Clausewitz agreed that you should only fight battles that are worth their price.

This builds directly on the earlier Sun Tzu readings. The five factors and calculation before battle, from Day 7, are how you decide whether the fight is winnable at all. Deception, from Day 12, is one of the main tools for attacking the enemy's plans. And there is a clean link to the Game Theory track: Day 13 covered Nash equilibrium, where each side picks its best response to what the other will do. Winning without fighting is really about shaping the game so that the opponent's best response is to stand down. Schelling, later in this track, built a whole theory of conflict on that idea.

Question for today: in a situation you are facing right now at work, what would it take for the other side to decide the fight is not worth having? Is that cheaper than winning the fight?

Optional source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, chapter 3, in either the Lionel Giles or Samuel Griffith translation. The first five sentences carry the whole idea.
